title: Inverted triangle pole top
description: Some poles in western Java carry only an inverted-triangle pole top, with no triangle connector under it. When a second layer sits below that top, the usual western Java triangle-connector rules apply again. Outside Java it is seen in Medan in North Sumatra, and it is relatively common in the Aceh coverage released in June 2024.

title: Crossbar-less pole with one insulator
description: A pole carrying a single insulator near its top, with no crossbar at all, is found only in Central Java and Yogyakarta. It occasionally doubles up to two insulators, the way every Indonesian pole type does from time to time.

title: T-shaped insulator arrangement
description: The insulators sit in an upside-down T: one raised on the pole above two on the crossbar. A second pole top underneath is most common in West Kalimantan, but the arrangement also turns up in Central Java.

title: Symmetric metal extension on a pole top
description: A metal extension sits on top of another pole top, held up by two vertical beams, with or without support beams. In Central Java and Yogyakarta it generally crowns a plain concrete pole; West Sumatra instead puts it on top of its own regional pole top.

title: Bulging asymmetric pole
description: The pole carries on well above the crossbar in a marked bulge. Spotting one gives well over a 90% chance of East Java, the rest being in and around South Kalimantan, notably in the fields near Banjarmasin.

title: Flattened insulators on a thick crossbar
description: South Kalimantan runs especially old electrical gear: the insulators look squashed and the crossbars are exceptionally thick. The type is most common in South Kalimantan and rare elsewhere in Kalimantan.

title: Short horizontal beam under the crossbar
description: A stubby horizontal metal beam bracing the pole just under the crossbar, on the generic asymmetric poles used throughout Kalimantan — West Kalimantan excepted, which has its own design.

title: Coloured bands on highway support poles
description: Support poles along the highways of Kalimantan carry painted bands whose colours split the provinces: pink and grey in Central Kalimantan, light purple and green in East Kalimantan.

title: Plain metal possum guard
description: A smooth metal sleeve wrapped round the pole, meant against snakes here rather than possums. Mostly South and East Kalimantan, with distinct designs in Jambi and on Bintan, and rare occurrences towards the east of West Java.

title: Possum guard with teeth and notches
description: A possum guard whose two ends are cut into teeth, with triangular notches in the middle of the sleeve. This design belongs to South Kalimantan.

title: Spiked possum guard
description: A metal sleeve bristling with long spikes pointing downwards, the most aggressive of the Indonesian possum guards. Found in South Kalimantan.

title: West Kalimantan symmetric metal pole
description: A symmetric pole made of metal, braced by two support beams at roughly 45 degrees. A version with a single support beam is still a West Kalimantan pole; concrete ones exist but are more common outside the province than in it.

title: Nusa pole: equal segments either side
description: The test for a true Nusa pole: the support beam cuts the crossbar so that the segment from the pole to that meeting point and the segment beyond it are the same length. This holds whether the pole is symmetric or asymmetric and whatever angle the support beam makes. Symmetric ones often carry a small bracket in the middle. Nusa Tenggara and Bali.

title: Nusa poles: concrete west, metal east
description: Within the family of long-support-beam Nusa poles, the material splits the islands: concrete poles are more common in West Nusa Tenggara and Bali, metal ones in East Nusa Tenggara.

title: Nusa pole with an extended base beam
description: A Nusa-type pole whose support beams rest on an extra horizontal beam running across the pole at their base. This variant belongs to southern Sumatra rather than to the Nusa islands themselves.

title: Off-centre Nusa pole of Sulawesi
description: Nusa-adjacent poles in Sulawesi are almost exclusively asymmetric, and are often strikingly off-centre or oversized, the crossbar sitting well to one side of the pole. Some, however, look perfectly ordinary.

title: North Maluku Nusa variant
description: Almost a true Nusa pole, but the pole and its support beam do not quite bisect the space between the central insulator and the outer one — the meeting point is visibly off. North Maluku.

title: Short support beams of southern Sulawesi
description: The support beams are shorter than the Indonesian average, so the gap between where the pole and where the support beam meet the crossbar is noticeably reduced. A variant that also brings the pole closer to the centre is mostly Southeast Sulawesi.

title: Support pole with a single yellow stripe
description: A support pole bearing nothing but one painted yellow band. It marks the main road through West Sulawesi, and since 2023 the main road around Balikpapan in East Kalimantan as well.

title: Octagonal pole
description: A concrete pole whose shaft is faceted rather than round. Octagonal poles are rare everywhere in Indonesia but make up about 6% of poles in North Maluku, with a scattering on all the major islands of East Nusa Tenggara, a few parts of Central Sulawesi and one road in southern Gorontalo.

title: Twisted support beams
description: A West-Kalimantan-like symmetric pole whose support beams are visibly twisted along their length. Found in North Maluku.

title: Pole top with a bracket in the middle
description: A West-Kalimantan-like pole carrying an extra bracket at the centre of the crossbar, between the support beams. North Maluku, and also South Sulawesi.

title: Bengkulu's false North Sumatra pole
description: A symmetric pole with one insulator on one side and two on the other — the usual North Sumatra rule — but found in Bengkulu and northern parts of southern Sumatra. The rule alone is not enough to place a pole in North Sumatra.

title: Curup pole
description: Like the bulging asymmetric pole of East Java, but always metal and with an extra ledge at the top of the bulge. It is most common in Bengkulu around the town of Curup. Northern Sulawesi has it too, where the ledge is longer and parallel to the pole top instead of perpendicular.

title: North Sumatra trident variant
description: A trident pole top with a wide head and a horizontal beam running between the two support beams. This variant is unique to North Sumatra.

title: Crossbar set entirely to one side
description: The whole crossbar sits on one side of the pole, balanced by a particularly long support beam. It turns up randomly in urban areas across the country, so it is worth something mainly when seen in rural or farming country, where it points to North Sumatra.

title: Thick shiny metal pole of West Sumatra
description: A symmetric metal pole, always metal, with a long horizontal beam between support beams that climb at about 60 degrees. West Sumatra's are notably thick and shiny — ignore the rust. Similar poles exist in West Kalimantan and northern Sulawesi.

title: Concrete pole with a long steep support beam
description: A concrete asymmetric pole whose single support beam is long and set at 60 to 75 degrees, meeting the crossbar halfway between the middle insulator and the pole. West Sumatra.

title: Pole rising just above its insulators
description: A less common West Sumatra variant: the support beam takes a more modest 45-degree angle, so the pole looks like a standard asymmetric one. The telltale is that the pole extends slightly above the level of the insulators.

title: Very tall pole with triangular wires
description: A pole far taller than anything else in the country, with small triangle-shaped wires running down its length. Entirely unique to Riau.

title: Huge squared X pylon
description: A twin-pole pylon braced by an X whose height and length are visibly equal, and either extremely tall or extremely wide — much more so than the X-poles used elsewhere in Indonesia. Entirely unique to Riau.

title: L-rod
description: A rod bent into an L, with a sharp 90-degree angle at its base, carrying a wire above the crossbar. L-rods are unique to the Riau Islands, mainland Riau and the Bangka-Belitung Islands, with exceptions in western Java, Southeast Sulawesi and West Sumatra.

title: Riau Islands split in two
description: The Riau Archipelago mostly shares its poles with mainland Riau, but divides: Batam and Bintan run almost entirely concrete poles, often with triangle connectors and L-rods, while Karimun and Kundur are more mixed and lean towards the metal poles of the mainland.

title: Insulator resting on top of a rod
description: A vertical rod rises from the pole top and carries a single insulator at its tip, above the crossbar. Unique to the Bangka-Belitung Islands, with one rare exception known in North Sumatra.

title: Pentagon-shaped rod on the pole top
description: A thin rod bent into a pentagon standing above the crossbar. Bangka-Belitung Islands, and quite rarely South and West Sumatra.

title: Aceh pole
description: The pole extends above the crossbar and is braced by two support beams at about 60 degrees. It can also carry a fairly long beam between the support beams, like the North Sumatra trident pole.

title: Two- and three-layer poles of urban Aceh
description: Urban Aceh stacks two or three crossbars on one pole. The top layer keeps the 60-degree support beams of the standard Aceh pole, while the lower layers drop to 45 degrees.

title: Yellow flap
description: Nearly every pole carries a small flap warning of the danger. All of the country except northern Sumatra uses white and yellow ones, though rust and dirt make them hard to tell apart. Sumatra, Kalimantan and Maluku are mostly yellow; Sulawesi and West Kalimantan mostly white; Java and Nusa Tenggara are largely mixed.

title: White clamped flap
description: A white flap clamped between two thick horizontal metal bars, one above and one below. Northern Sulawesi — North Sulawesi, Gorontalo and Central Sulawesi — where Central Sulawesi most often places it near the crossbar.

title: Flap bolted at its four corners
description: A white flap fixed flat to the pole by a bolt in each corner. West Kalimantan, where the southern highway uses yellow flaps of the same design instead.

title: Long flap with a yellow logo
description: A longer white flap carrying more text than usual and a yellow rectangular logo in the middle of it. West Sumatra.

title: Papua and Maluku poles
description: Coverage is still thin, but most poles there follow the West Kalimantan pattern: symmetric, metal, two support beams. Asymmetric poles appear around Nabire in Central Papua, and large coils are sometimes fitted under the support beam.

title: Triangle connector of West Java/Riau
description:
Western Java’s poles often have triangle connectors, a rod with a 135º angle, and/or a large indentation resembling those of poles found in Chile.
Note that triangle connectors may be found elsewhere in Indonesia.

title: Central Java insulator
description:
Key characteristics:
No crossbar
One insulator at the top

May occasionally have two insulators, reflecting how all types of poles “double up”
